big_idea: The 2s, 5s, and 10s multiplication facts are anchors.
learning_intention: We are learning to recall multiplication facts of 2, 5, and 10 and to write the related division facts.
student_learning_goal: I can recall multiplication facts of 2, 5, and 10 and write the related division facts.
success_criteria: I can recall any ×2, ×5, ×10 fact within 3 seconds.
I can write all 4 facts of a fact-family triangle.
I can use a known multiplication to solve a division (5×6=30, so 30÷5=6).
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Maya the Multiplication Maven — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Anchor chart 'Fact Families: 2s, 5s, 10s' with sample triangles
Per-pair set of array grid + counters
Fact Triangle deck (30 cards focused on 2s, 5s, 10s)
Lesson 2 fact-recall tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Maya has 4 rows of 5 stickers. How many altogether? AND what's the related division? Maya opens: 'Skip-count UP, multiplication's the SUM!' Pixel taps the toolkit: 'Tools work better with PRACTICE!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Maya the Multiplication Maven puppet in hand. 'Friends — meet Maya. She runs the multiplication side of the Toolkit.'

Show an array grid with 4 rows × 5 columns of counters. 'Maya has 4 rows of 5 stickers. How many altogether?' '4 × 5 = 20.' Write on the board.

'Maya says — every multiplication has SIBLINGS. Watch.' Same array. 'I can also see 5 rows of 4 (rotate the array). 5 × 4 = 20.' Write.

'And division.' '20 stickers shared into 4 rows = 5 each. 20 ÷ 4 = 5.' Write. '20 stickers shared into 5 rows = 4 each. 20 ÷ 5 = 4.' Write.

Four facts:
4 × 5 = 20
5 × 4 = 20
20 ÷ 4 = 5
20 ÷ 5 = 4

'This is a FACT FAMILY. Three numbers — 4, 5, 20 — make 4 facts. Maya says — if you know ONE, you know FOUR.'

Show the fact triangle: 20 at the top, 4 and 5 at the bottom corners.

Now rapid-fire ×2, ×5, ×10. '2 × 7?' '14.' '5 × 6?' '30.' '10 × 8?' '80.' '5 × 9?' '45.' '2 × 6?' '12.'

'Today we'll lock in the ×2, ×5, ×10 facts AND the related divisions.'
student_actions: Help find the four facts in the triangle.

steps.instruction: Whole group: practice 5 more fact families. (a) 2×8=16 (and 16÷2, 16÷8). (b) 5×7=35. (c) 10×6=60. (d) 2×9=18. (e) 5×4=20.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Five more triangles together. Tell me all 4 facts each.'

steps.instruction: Send pairs to three stations (~7 min each). Station A: Array Build — pair has counters and array grid; teacher gives a fact, pair builds the array, writes all 4 facts. Station B: Fact Triangle Race — pair takes turns flashing a triangle; partner writes all 4 facts within 30 seconds. Station C: Multiplication Chart Hunt — pair has the 1-10 chart; highlight all the ×2, ×5, ×10 rows and notice patterns.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Three stations, 7 minutes each.'

steps.instruction: Stretch challenge at Station B: include 4 facts from outside ×2, ×5, ×10 (e.g., 3×4, 6×7) — children apply the fact-family logic even on unfamiliar facts.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to pairs at Station B: 'Some triangles use facts you don't know yet. Try to figure out all 4 facts using arrays.'

steps.instruction: Discuss the relationship. 'Why does 5 × 4 equal 4 × 5?' (Commutative — same array, viewed differently.) 'Why does knowing 5 × 4 help with 20 ÷ 4?' (Inverse — division undoes multiplication.)
steps.teacher_prompt: Use arrays to demonstrate both. Tilt the array 90 degrees for commutativity; reverse the count for inverse.

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the fact-recall tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Flash a fact and time silently.

steps.instruction: STRATEGY COMPARE: Two pairs share their toolkit approaches — skip-count vs known-fact recall vs array drawing. Class compares for 6×5: which is fastest? Cite Carpenter, Fennema & Franke (1996) CGI on derived facts.
steps.teacher_prompt: Maya: 'Three tools, same answer. Pick the tool your brain trusts.'

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at Station A. Use only ×2 facts (the smallest multiples).
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch to ×3, ×4. Discuss whether these are also fact families (yes — every multiplication is).
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide picture-supported triangles. Pair with a strong-recall peer for Station B.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Skip-count by 2s, 5s, 10s while walking. Body-on-floor reinforces the multiplication-as-skip-count link. NO-PAPER VERSION: children skip-count by 2s/5s/10s using fingers + claps. Body becomes the multiplication tool.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: recalls ×2/×5/×10 facts within 3 seconds; writes all 4 facts of a fact-family triangle; uses multiplication to solve division (and vice versa).
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the fact-recall tracker per child.
tracker_columns: Writes all 4 facts of a triangle

discussion_prompts: If 5 × 8 = 40, what other facts do you know?
Why does multiplying by 10 always give a number ending in 0?
consolidation.exit_routine: Maya's toolkit refrain — 'Skip-count UP, multiplication's the SUM!' (3x). Each child writes one multiplication fact + its inverse division on a sticky. Pixel's tap-out: '2s, 5s, 10s — practice makes them STICK!'

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Fluency on ×2, ×5, ×10 facts; fact-family completion accuracy.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 2 captures B2.2 mastery for the gateway facts. Children at L4 are fluent on all three (×2, ×5, ×10) and connect every multiplication to its division partner.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child knows 5 × 8 = 40 but cannot solve 40 ÷ 5 — repairing the multiplication-division separation
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On multiplication facts (2s, 5s, 10s), the trap is multiplication-division separation: child can recite 5×3=15 but cannot answer 15÷5 (Carpenter, Fennema & Franke 1996 CGI; Anghileri 2001). Without inverse fluency, Lesson 3 (10×10) and Lesson 4 (numerator) cannot ground.

Yesterday Tony's regrouping. Today Maya's multiplication toolkit. Lesson 3 to 10×10; Lesson 4 fractions; Lesson 5 ratios.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station B. Maya flashes triangle (5, 8, 40). The child writes 5 × 8 = 40 confidently, then 8 × 5 = 40. They look stuck on the division facts.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the child. 'Great — you got both multiplications. Now divisions.' The child says 'I don't know 40 ÷ 5.' Pause. 'But you JUST said 5 × 8 = 40. So 40 ÷ 5 = ?' The child still hesitates.

'Watch.' Build 5 × 8 with counters: 5 rows × 8 columns. 'When we MULTIPLY, we count rows times columns: 5 × 8 = 40. When we DIVIDE, we go BACKWARDS — we know the total (40) and the number of rows (5), so we count COLUMNS. 40 ÷ 5 means take 40 things and arrange them in 5 rows. How many in each row?' Point to the array. '8 in each row.' '40 ÷ 5 = 8.'

Now the rule. 'Maya says — every triangle holds the same THREE numbers, but used differently. The TOP number (40) is the product OR the dividend. The TWO BOTTOM numbers are the factors OR the divisor and quotient.'

Have the child redo. 'Now 40 ÷ 8 = ?' '5.' Affirm.

If the child STILL separates the operations: practice with smaller fact triangles first. (3, 4, 12): 3×4=12, 4×3=12, 12÷3=4, 12÷4=3. Build until they auto-flip.

Long-term recovery: every multiplication practice = also write the division. Two pairs of facts per triangle. Daily.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Knows multiplications but freezes on related divisions. Most common at start of Lesson 2.
(Mid) Solves division with prompts about the related multiplication.
(Strong) Auto-flips: '5 × 8 = 40, so 40 ÷ 5 = 8 and 40 ÷ 8 = 5.' All four facts within 5 seconds.
(Stretched) Volunteers all four facts immediately when given any one. Sees triangles structurally.
common_misconceptions: Multiplication and division are different operations. (Repair: arrays show they're inverses.)
Division is just subtraction. (Some Grade-3 hold-overs treat 40÷5 as 'subtract 5 until you reach 0'. Correct technically — gets 8 — but the multiplication-recall route is faster.)
Fact families always have 4 facts. (Doubles like 5×5=25 have only 3 facts: 5×5=25, 25÷5=5. Repair: explicit doubles-special-case.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child recites multiplication but blanks on division: drill 'inverse fact' — '5×3 = 15, so 15÷5 = 3 AND 15÷3 = 5'; physical demo with arrays.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child counts by 2s/5s/10s but stalls beyond 10×: chunk 'count by 5s ten times = 50; that's 5×10'.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child computes but cannot articulate: force the sentence frame 'I know 4×5 = 20 because 4 groups of 5 equals 20.'

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of B2.2 (×2, ×5, ×10 + related divisions) and B2.1 (fact families).

parts_outline.task: Fluency table: 12 facts across ×2, ×5, ×10. Child fills in answers.
Six fact triangles. Child writes all 4 facts (or 3 for doubles).
Six division facts. Child writes the related multiplication for each.

expected_image_assets: Maya the Multiplication Maven in the worksheet header
